top_picks.name: Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
top_picks.thesis: You like ETFs because you own the whole field without betting the farm on one company, and this week keeps making the case. VOO holds the 500 largest US companies for a rock-bottom 0.03% fee. Today the selling was surgical rather than broad: the AI hardware chain was liquidated (Vertiv -16% on an earnings timing miss, Nebius -10%, KLA -8%, Micron -7%, the chip ETF SMH -2.4% on 1.47x volume and its 11th distribution day), while healthcare and dividend value closed at the very top of their 30-day ranges and Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet all rose. The index fell only 0.72%, because the money rotated inside VOO rather than leaving it. That is the entire argument for owning the whole field: you held the winners and the losers of the rotation simultaneously, and the net was a rounding error. VOO now sits at 15% of its 30-day range and fractionally below its 50-day, which is a perfectly ordinary place to keep buying.
top_picks.why_now: The macro backdrop just changed in a way that argues for the core over the satellites. The Fed held at 3.50-3.75% this afternoon, but three officials dissented in favor of a HIKE, and futures now put roughly 76% odds on a September increase, up from 59% a month ago. The driver is energy: WTI crude is back near $84, up about 16% in a month on the Iran conflict, which pushed the 10-year Treasury to 4.65% after a 2026 high near 4.71%. Core inflation is still cooling (June CPI 3.5%, core 2.6%), so this is an energy shock on top of real disinflation, not a broad re-acceleration. When the rate path is genuinely two-sided and Goldman's prime desk is reporting the largest hedge-fund retreat from tech in over a decade, guessing which layer gets sold next is a losing game. Owning all 500 is not. Keep the fixed dollar-cost-average running on schedule and let the rotation happen inside the fund.
top_picks.risk: Because the top handful of mega-cap tech names are roughly a third of the S&P, an AI-capex or return-on-investment scare is the one shock that can drag the whole index, even though today the damage stayed in the supplier layer. The spending is now partly debt-funded (hyperscalers are tapping external financing as capex outruns operating cash flow), which makes the whole complex more rate-sensitive than it was a year ago. So a September hike would hit it twice. The index can also pull back if the 10-year, now 4.65%, grinds toward 5%. The fix is time and steady contributions, not timing the top. VTI (total US market, same 0.03% fee) is a near-identical alternative that adds mid and small caps.

insights.title: The broadest flush yet: 14 of 62 names logged heavy institutional selling
insights.body: This is the widest liquidation signal the board has shown in this stretch. Fourteen of the 62 watchlist names registered a heavy-liquidation event (a big down day on far above-average volume), and the damage is concentrated in one place: the AI hardware chain. The semiconductor ETF SMH fell about 2.4% on 1.47x normal volume, now carrying 11 distribution days and two heavy events, sitting at the very bottom of its 30-day range and about 11% below its 50-day average. SOXX is worse against its 50-day at roughly -13.5% on 1.49x volume. Fiber optics is the epicenter: Corning traded 3.58x its average volume and sits about 32% under its 50-day, with Coherent at -31% and Ciena at -26%. Memory is right behind (SanDisk -36% vs its 50-day with 11 distribution days, Micron -7% on the day). Individual wreckage was severe: Vertiv -16%, Nebius -10%, KLA -8%, Micron -7%, Atkore -6.8%, CoreWeave -6.6%, Super Micro -6.3%. The contrast is the whole story. While that was happening, the S&P proxy SPY fell only 0.72% and sits just 0.5% under its 50-day, because the money did not leave the market, it moved. Healthcare (XLV) and dividend value (SCHD) both closed at the very top of their 30-day ranges, and Apple, AbbVie, Merck and Johnson & Johnson all sit at or near 30-day highs.
insights.matters: Heavy volume on down days is institutions selling, not retail noise, and when it clusters this widely it usually means positions are being cut rather than trimmed. But note what did NOT happen: the index barely moved. That is rotation, not a market break. For a long-term buyer the practical read is that the AI hardware layer is being priced for a slowdown while defensives are being bid to the top of their ranges, which is historically a better moment to be adding slowly to the beaten-down layer (SMH, SOXX) than chasing the crowded one. Keep the fixed contributions going into the diversified core (VOO, VTI), and if you want AI hardware exposure, buy it in thirds rather than at once: 11 distribution days says the selling may not be finished.

insights.title: The Fed held, but three officials voted to raise and September hike odds jumped to about 76%
insights.body: The FOMC left the benchmark rate at 3.50% to 3.75% this afternoon, the fifth straight meeting without a change and the second under Chair Kevin Warsh. The headline is not the hold, it is the dissents: three regional presidents (Beth Hammack of Cleveland, Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis, Lorie Logan of Dallas) voted for a HIKE. That is an unusually large hawkish bloc, and the market repriced accordingly: futures now put roughly 76% odds on a rate increase in September, up from about 59% a month ago. Warsh has said the committee will not hesitate to act if inflation pressures accelerate. The bond market had already been leaning that way. The 10-year Treasury sits at 4.65% (it touched about 4.71% last week, the highest of 2026), up from 4.40% a month ago, while the 2-year is 4.31%, leaving the 10Y-2Y curve positively sloped at about +34 basis points. VIX at 18.2 says the equity market is uneasy but not panicked.
insights.matters: For most of the last two years the working assumption was that the next move is a cut. That assumption is now genuinely in question, and it changes what works. A higher-for-longer or higher-from-here rate path pressures long-duration growth hardest, which is exactly the layer being liquidated (chips, fiber, neoclouds, the pre-revenue nuclear and space developers), and rewards balance-sheet strength and cash flow you get paid today. That is the mechanical reason SCHD, XLV, AbbVie and Merck are pinned at the top of their ranges. Practical takeaway: do not lower your cash yield assumptions yet, keep some dry powder earning interest, and favor low-debt names when you add. The Aug 12 CPI print is now a live event rather than a formality.

insights.title: Oil back near $84 is the reason the Fed turned hawkish, and the reason yields hit 2026 highs
insights.body: West Texas Intermediate crude sits at about $84 a barrel, up roughly 16% from $72.67 a month ago, driven by escalating conflict involving Iran. That single move is doing most of the work in this macro picture. It pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to its highest level of 2026 last week, it is the specific pressure the three dissenting Fed officials pointed at, and it is why an Aug 12 CPI print that would otherwise be routine now carries real consequence. The underlying inflation data is still improving: June headline CPI came in at 3.5% year over year (down from 4.2%) and core CPI at 2.6% (down from 2.8%), with unemployment steady at 4.2%. So the disinflation trend has not broken. But energy feeds through to headline inflation with a lag of a month or two, and July is the month that will show it.
insights.matters: This is the classic late-cycle bind: the core trend says the Fed is winning, the energy shock says wait. For a long-term investor the useful response is not to trade the oil headline, it is to make sure the portfolio is not built entirely on the assumption that rates fall. Businesses that can pass costs through (healthcare, market-priced power operators like Constellation and Vistra) and broad diversified exposure (VOO, VTI) both handle an energy-driven inflation bump better than pre-revenue growth. If the Aug 12 print comes in hot on energy, expect another leg of exactly the rotation you saw today. If it comes in soft, the beaten-down AI hardware layer is where the snapback would be sharpest, which is an argument for owning some of it rather than none.

insights.title: Vertiv beat on earnings, raised full-year guidance, and still fell 16%
insights.body: Vertiv, the data-center cooling and power specialist, is the cleanest illustration of the mood shift. It reported Q2 earnings per share of $1.52 against a $1.42 estimate, grew organic sales 18%, and RAISED its full-year outlook to $13.8-14.2 billion in sales and $6.65-6.75 in EPS, citing expanding customer pipelines. The stock fell about 16%. The sole offense was revenue of $3.27 billion against a $3.37 billion consensus, which management attributed to minor timing shifts from supply-chain congestion and multi-phase project execution as AI deployments get larger. After a roughly 67% year-to-date run into the print, that was enough. This follows Alphabet, whose stock fell 7% last week when it raised its capex guide and reported the first negative quarterly free cash flow in company history. Combined 2026 capex commitments across Amazon (~$200B), Alphabet ($175-185B), Microsoft ($120B+) and Meta ($115-135B) now sit around $725-785 billion, up roughly 77% year over year.
insights.matters: The demand is not in question, the market's patience with the timeline is. A year ago a raised guide was rewarded; today a one-quarter revenue slip inside a raised guide costs you 16%. That is what a show-me-the-return regime looks like, and it means the AI infrastructure names will keep having violent single-day moves on ordinary operational noise. For a long-term holder this is an argument for the basket over the single name: SMH and SOXX spread that headline risk across 25-30 companies, so one Vertiv-style gap does not wreck the position. It is also a reminder to check the run-up before an earnings date. A name up 67% year to date is priced for perfection whatever the fundamentals say.

insights.title: Nuclear rolled over across the board: the operators cracked and the developers kept bleeding
insights.body: The nuclear trade lost its last pocket of strength. The uranium ETF URA fell 2.4% and sits about 13.5% below its 50-day; VanEck's NLR is 11.4% below with seven distribution days. What changed is that the damage is no longer confined to the speculative end. Vistra fell 3.4% and GE Vernova 3.2%, both on heavy liquidation volume, and both are now at the bottom of their 30-day ranges. Cameco, the mature uranium producer, has accumulated eight distribution days and sits 13.7% under its 50-day. Constellation is the lone holdout, up 0.6% and roughly flat to its 50-day. The developers are far worse: Oklo is down about 28% against its 50-day with six distribution days, and BWXT fell 5.6%. Reporting through July has framed this as investors rotating out of AI-linked trades and demanding evidence that advanced reactor companies can actually hit their milestones. Oklo does not expect its first Aurora Powerhouse online until late 2027 or early 2028.
insights.matters: The distinction that matters for a long-term buyer is cash flow today versus a promise for 2028. Constellation and Vistra sell power now into a market where data-center demand is genuinely growing, so their selloff is a valuation reset inside a working business. Oklo, NuScale and the fuel developers are still pre-revenue bets on execution, and in a regime where the Fed may hike, those are precisely the assets that get repriced hardest, because their value sits far in the future. If you believe the electricity thesis (and the hyperscaler capex numbers support it), the disciplined expression is the operators or a fund like NLR, sized as a real position, with the developers sized as small speculative bets you can afford to see cut in half. Do not average down aggressively into a name whose first revenue is two years away.

insights.title: Space and quantum took the worst of it: size these like venture bets, not positions
insights.body: The speculative end of the board is where the rate repricing lands hardest, and the numbers are stark. Intuitive Machines sits about 49% below its 50-day average and fell 5.8% on the day. Rocket Lab is 36.5% below its 50-day. The space ETF UFO is down 15.4% versus its 50-day. In quantum, Rigetti fell 6.1% and is 24.8% under its 50-day, and the quantum baskets QTUM and WQTM are 11.3% and 15.3% below theirs respectively. The AI neoclouds belong in this bucket too: Nebius fell 10% on 1.55x volume with seven distribution days and sits 24.8% below its 50-day, CoreWeave fell 6.6% and is 29.8% below. The government-backed materials names are in the same boat, with MP Materials down 5.7% on heavy volume and 25.9% below its 50-day, and Lithium Americas 32.2% below.
insights.matters: None of these are broken theses, and several carry government backing (MP, Lithium Americas, Rocket Lab, BWXT and LEU all carry GOV badges on this board for a reason). But they share one property: their value depends almost entirely on cash flows years out, which is the exact thing a hawkish Fed discounts hardest. The rule that keeps you solvent through this is position sizing, not conviction. Any single frontier name should be small enough that a 50% drawdown is annoying rather than portfolio-altering, because drawdowns of that size have already happened here. If you want the theme with less single-name risk, the baskets (QTUM, UFO, and ITA for defense, which is actually holding up at 73% of its range) spread the failure risk. Everything above the frontier sleeve should still be the boring core.

smart_money.intro: Where the large, informed money is actually positioned. This is a timing tool and a sanity check, never a reason to buy or sell on its own: institutions are wrong regularly, they operate on far shorter horizons than you do, and by the time these filings are public the trade is often weeks old. Read it as context for how crowded a trade is, not as a signal.

items.title: Goldman's desk: the record tech selling is still running, and capitulation signs are emerging
items.body: Goldman Sachs Prime Services reports that hedge funds have pulled back from US technology at a record pace over the past two months. The cohort was a net seller of the sector in six of the last eight weeks, and the cumulative reduction in market value totals roughly 10%, the largest retreat from tech since the data series began more than a decade ago. Goldman's own language notes that the persistence and magnitude of the selling since early June point to significant length reduction, and that some signs of capitulation are starting to emerge. Where the money went: commercial services, consumer staples, real estate and energy, plus broad index and ETF products. Semiconductors led the outflows. Note that Goldman's prime brokerage data itself is proprietary and is read here through public reporting on it.
items.matters: This corroborates the volume data on your own board from a completely independent source: 14 heavy liquidation events and 11 distribution days on SMH is what a record de-grossing looks like from the inside. The phrase worth holding onto is capitulation. Forced selling by leveraged players is mechanical rather than fundamental, and it historically ends by exhausting itself, not by good news arriving. That does not tell you the bottom is in, and it is not a reason to rush. It is a reason to keep your scheduled contributions running into weakness rather than pausing them, which is the single behavior that separates long-term investors from the funds doing the selling.

items.title: Positioning unchanged this week: the Jul 21 report still stands, with leveraged funds short the Nasdaq
items.body: The CFTC's weekly Traders in Financial Futures data has not refreshed since the last briefing; the Jul 21 report is still the most recent, and the next release lands Friday Jul 31. As of Jul 21, asset managers (the long-horizon institutional money, closest to how you invest) remain heavily net long: +929,159 contracts in S&P 500 e-minis, roughly 48% of open interest, and +72,625 in Nasdaq-100 e-minis. Leveraged funds (the fast, hedged money) are on the other side, net short 322,865 S&P contracts and 74,690 Nasdaq contracts. The week-over-week direction is the interesting part: leveraged funds COVERED 42,137 S&P shorts while ADDING 10,527 Nasdaq shorts. In Treasuries, asset managers added 24,755 contracts to an already enormous 10-year note long. In VIX futures, leveraged funds cut 7,091 contracts of long volatility.
items.matters: The split between the two cohorts is the signal. Fast money is pressing bets specifically against the Nasdaq while easing off the broad S&P, which lines up precisely with the tape: a chip and AI-hardware flush inside a broad index that barely moved. Long-horizon institutional money has not blinked and stays heavily long both indices, which matters more for someone with your time frame. Treat this as confirmation that the selling is concentrated and tactical rather than a broad institutional exit. Since the data is now eight days stale and predates today's Fed decision, do not lean on it hard until Friday's refresh.

items.title: Policy money keeps flowing to power, defense and domestic materials while the market sells them
items.body: The policy tailwinds under several beaten-down parts of this board have not changed, even as prices have. The Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program continues to back advanced reactor developers including Oklo, which also holds a power-campus commitment from Meta. The GOV badges on this board flag where the US government either holds equity (Intel, MP Materials, Lithium Americas) or is the anchor customer (Centrus, BWXT, Rocket Lab, Palantir). Every one of the equity-stake names sold off today, with MP down 5.7% on heavy volume and Intel logging its own heavy liquidation event and eight distribution days. Defense is the exception that proves the pattern: ITA sits at 73% of its 30-day range and 4.6% above its 50-day, holding up while the rest of the government-linked complex fell.
items.matters: A government equity stake or anchor contract is a floor under the business, not a floor under the stock price, and this week made the difference concrete. It reduces the odds of the company failing outright, which is exactly why these names can be owned at all in a speculative sleeve, but it does nothing to stop a valuation reset when rates rise. The takeaway is to use the GOV badge as a survivability filter when choosing which speculative names to own, and to use position sizing to handle the volatility that comes with them anyway. It is a signal, not a guarantee.

items.title: The spenders keep raising budgets even as their own shareholders punish them for it
items.body: The four largest AI spenders have committed roughly $725-785 billion of 2026 capital expenditure, up about 77% year over year: Amazon near $200 billion, Alphabet $175-185 billion, Microsoft above $120 billion, Meta $115-135 billion. Consensus estimates put the group above $1 trillion annually as soon as next year. What shifted is the market's reception. Alphabet raised its capex guide alongside Q2 results, reported the first negative quarterly free cash flow in its history, and the stock fell 7%. Amazon, Meta and Microsoft all fell in sympathy on scrutiny of returns. Reporting notes the group is increasingly tapping external financing because the buildout is outrunning operating cash flow. On your board the hyperscalers themselves are holding up better than their suppliers: Microsoft rose 0.8% and Alphabet 1.2% today, while the companies selling them cooling, fiber and memory were liquidated.
items.matters: The order book behind your AI infrastructure holdings is not shrinking, it is growing, and that is the single most important fact for anyone holding SMH or the picks-and-shovels names through this drawdown. What the market is repricing is the timeline and the financing, not the demand. Two practical consequences. The buildout is now partly debt-funded, which makes it more sensitive to the rate path than it was a year ago, so a September Fed hike would hit this complex twice. And the spenders being rewarded while the suppliers are sold means owning the customer (Microsoft, Alphabet, or simply VOO, which holds them all) has been the lower-volatility way to own the same theme.

primer.intro: A large AI data center is a machine built in physical layers, and money flows into it from the top (the customers who order it) down through every supplier who makes a piece. Here is where the dollars land, and why the least glamorous layers can be the safest way to invest.

sections.h: Start at the top: the customers
sections.p: The hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle) announce the giant spending budgets, now roughly $700-725B in 2026, that everyone else competes to capture. Owning them is the most diversified way to own the theme, because their core businesses (ads, cloud, software) fund the AI bet and keep earning even if AI spending pauses. Two cautions surfaced this quarter: the market is now scrutinizing the return on that capex (Alphabet raised its 2026 spend and its free cash flow turned negative), and Meta revealed it has excess compute to resell, a reminder that even well-funded buyers can build ahead of demand.

Nvidia (NVDA) designs the GPUs that do the AI math; AMD (AMD) is the challenger; Broadcom (AVGO) builds the custom chips hyperscalers increasingly design in-house, a trend now challenging Nvidia's near-monopoly. None own factories: TSMC (TSM) prints the chips using machines only ASML (ASML) makes, and every GPU needs memory from Micron (MU). Highest growth, highest risk, and the layer that falls first on any overcapacity or competition scare, as this month proved when a Chinese memory IPO (ChangXin) reset the whole DRAM and NAND trade.

sections.h: Layer 2: The box and the room
sections.p: The chips get assembled into servers by Super Micro (SMCI) and Dell (DELL). A rack of AI chips runs blazing hot, so it needs advanced cooling and power distribution from Vertiv (VRT), and fast switches from Arista (ANET) to connect racks together. This is the guts of the room.

AI splits one job across thousands of chips, so they must talk at the speed of light over fiber. Transceivers and lasers come from Coherent (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE), long-haul interconnect from Ciena (CIEN), and the actual glass fiber from Corning (GLW). Optics content rises with every hardware generation, though these names trade with the chip complex on risk-off days like today's memory scare.

The least glamorous and often most attractive layer: switchgear from Eaton (ETN) and Hubbell (HUBB), the steel and PVC conduit that carries every wire from Atkore (ATKR), jobsite supply from WESCO (WCC), transmission and substation build from Quanta (PWR), and the raw steel from Nucor (NUE). Physical, hard-to-substitute, multi-year backlogs.

A data center is useless without electricity, and AI has made power the true bottleneck. Existing-reactor operators signing long deals are Constellation (CEG) and Vistra (VST); fuel comes from Cameco (CCJ); reactor and SMR technology from BWX (BWXT), Oklo (OKLO) and NuScale (SMR); and near-term gas-turbine and grid power from GE Vernova (GEV). The operators have held up far better than the developers through this quarter's selloffs, sitting near the tops of their ranges while the developers stay pinned near their lows.

Follow a dollar of capex: it lands most heavily on the chip layer, which captures the most dollars but carries the most risk (a rival can win a socket, custom silicon can erode the moat, a new supplier like China's ChangXin can pressure memory pricing, and an overcapacity or return-on-investment scare hits it first). The power, conduit, cooling and fiber layers are lower-binary: whatever chip and model win, the building still needs steel, copper, transformers and megawatts. That is the trade-off, highest upside in silicon, more durable margins of safety in the infrastructure beneath it.

macro_strategy.regime_label: Hawkish hold with an oil-driven inflation scare, and a record de-grossing running through AI hardware
macro_strategy.regime_detail: Three things define this tape. First, the Fed held at 3.50-3.75% today but three officials dissented for a HIKE, and futures now price roughly 76% odds of an increase in September, up from 59% a month ago. The two-year assumption that the next move is a cut is genuinely in question. Second, the cause is energy: WTI crude is back near $84, up about 16% in a month on the Iran conflict, which pushed the 10-year Treasury to 4.65% (a 2026 high of about 4.71% last week) and makes the Aug 12 CPI print a live event. The core trend is still improving (June CPI 3.5%, core 2.6%, unemployment 4.2%), so this is an energy shock layered on genuine disinflation, not a return of broad inflation. Third, positioning: Goldman's prime desk reports the largest hedge-fund retreat from tech in more than a decade, and your own board confirms it with 14 heavy liquidation events and 11 distribution days on SMH. The result is a market that is rotating violently rather than falling: SPY is down only 0.5% from its 50-day while semis are down 11% and fiber is down 30%, and healthcare and dividend value sit at the tops of their ranges. That rewards cash flow you get paid today, balance-sheet strength, and steady contributions into the diversified core over any attempt to time the AI layer.

drivers.reading: Hawkish hold with a live hike risk. Fed funds at 3.50-3.75% for a fifth straight meeting, but three presidents (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) dissented for a hike and September hike odds are near 76%. The 10-year sits at 4.65% after touching about 4.71%, the 2-year at 4.31%, and the 10Y-2Y curve is positively sloped at roughly +34 basis points. VIX at 18.2.
drivers.playbook: Stop planning around a cut. A flat-to-higher path pressures long-duration growth hardest, which is why the chips, fiber, neoclouds and pre-revenue nuclear names are the ones breaking, and why dividend value (SCHD) and healthcare (XLV, ABBV, MRK) are pinned at range highs. Favor low debt-to-equity when you add, keep meaningful cash earning its yield rather than forcing it into the market, and treat any move in the 10-year back under about 4.4% as the signal that pressure is easing.

drivers.reading: Core still cooling, headline at risk from energy. June CPI 3.5% (from 4.2%) and core 2.6% (from 2.8%), but WTI crude is back near $84, up roughly 16% in a month on the Iran conflict. Energy passes into headline inflation with a one-to-two-month lag, so the Aug 12 July print is where it shows up.
drivers.playbook: Own some pricing power and real assets: market-priced power operators (CEG, VST), healthcare that passes costs through, and broad exposure via VOO or VTI. Do not press risk into the Aug 12 print. A hot energy-driven number extends today's rotation, a soft one is where the beaten-down AI hardware layer snaps back hardest, which is the argument for holding some of it rather than none.

drivers.reading: Still resilient underneath a violently rotating tape. Unemployment is steady at 4.2%, hyperscaler capex commitments are rising toward $725-785 billion for 2026, and Vertiv grew organic sales 18% and raised guidance on the same day its stock fell 16%. The weakness is in multiples and positioning, not in demand.
drivers.playbook: Keep beta moderate and anchor on the diversified core (VOO, VTI) plus the defensive leadership (XLV or LLY, power operators CEG and VST). Size the high-beta AI sleeve (SMH, SOXX) so you can hold it through a 30% to 45% drawdown without selling, because that is the historical range for this group. Buy the liquidated layer in thirds over several weeks rather than at once: 11 distribution days says the selling is not necessarily finished.

macro_strategy.positioning: Core first: keep the fixed dollar-cost-average running into VOO or VTI regardless of the headlines, since the index fell only 0.7% on a day the chip complex was flushed and that is exactly the protection you pay for. Defensive sleeve: healthcare (XLV, or LLY and ABBV individually) and dividend value (SCHD) are working, but they are extended at the tops of their ranges, so hold and keep contributing rather than chasing. Opportunity sleeve: the AI hardware layer (SMH, SOXX) is at the bottom of its 30-day range on record institutional selling with demand still growing, which is a scale-in-slowly setup, not a back-up-the-truck one. Speculative sleeve: keep the frontier names (OKLO, quantum, space, neoclouds, MP, LAC) small enough that a 50% drawdown is survivable, because several have already delivered one. Cash: still earning a real yield with a hike genuinely possible, so patience costs you very little right now.

scenarios.trigger: If the Iran conflict de-escalates, oil falls back toward the low 70s, and the Aug 12 CPI print lands soft
scenarios.response: Risk-on, and the September hike gets priced back out. The 10-year eases below about 4.4%, and the layer that fell furthest snaps back hardest: add to the chip and fiber pullback (SMH, SOXX) in tranches, and let the ETF core, healthcare and power operators ride. This is the scenario that rewards having owned some AI hardware through the flush rather than none.

scenarios.trigger: If energy pushes the July CPI print higher and the Fed hikes in September, or the 10-year grinds toward 5%
scenarios.response: Risk-off, and the debt-funded part of the AI buildout gets repriced a second time. Lean into value, dividends and cash flows you collect today (SCHD, ABBV, MRK), keep the healthcare and power-operator leadership, pause the SMH scale-in, and hold dry powder: with a hike live, cash is still paying you to wait. The index itself is vulnerable here, because mega-cap tech is roughly a third of it.

scenarios.trigger: If the capex-ROI scrutiny spreads (more Vertiv-style timing misses, a hyperscaler finally trimming its guide, or the external financing getting more expensive)
scenarios.response: Risk-off in AI infrastructure specifically, even if the broad market holds. Lean harder on the diversified core (VOO), healthcare (XLV, LLY) and the power operators with revenue today (CEG, VST), favor the customers over the suppliers, and cut the speculative sleeve (neoclouds, pre-revenue nuclear, quantum, space) to sizes you can hold through another halving without selling.

watchlist_notes: Two sheets, same columns. Sheet 1 is the established, large-dollar side (semis and fab, chip equipment, memory and storage, servers and cooling, fiber, electrical and steel, nuclear and power majors, big tech, healthcare). Sheet 2 is the smaller-dollar speculative side (nuclear developers and fuel, quantum, space and defense, government-backed materials, small AI infra, neoclouds). Read the Bull Score first: it is six checks on whether the long-term case holds, and hovering it shows which checks passed. What the board looks like today: the AI hardware chain is at the bottom of its ranges almost everywhere, with fiber the worst hit (Corning about 32% below its 50-day on 3.58x volume, Coherent -31%, Ciena -26%), memory next (SanDisk -36% with 11 distribution days, Micron -14%), and chip equipment close behind (Lam -20%, KLA -14%). Fourteen of 62 names logged heavy institutional liquidation. The opposite corner is crowded: AbbVie, Merck, Apple, Nucor and Atkore all sit at 100% of their 30-day range, with Johnson & Johnson at 97%. Oracle carries the most distribution days on the board at 14 and sits 29% below its 50-day, which is worth watching as a single-name warning rather than a sector one. GOV badges mark where the US government holds equity (INTC, MP, LAC) or is the anchor customer (LEU, BWXT, RKLB, PLTR); most of those sold off today, which is a reminder that a government stake supports the business, not the share price. Not financial advice.
